text: “— What Cvetko told,” said the shy Ilcho, “that’s a later matter, and I know that Bay Ganyo had come to Prague earlier, had stayed there a long time, and had sold quite a lot of rose oil. Would you like me to tell you about it?”
— If it’s about Bay Ganya, don’t ask, just tell it! — we replied.

— Good. Listen then. Bay Ganyo arrives from Vienna in Prague. He gets off at the station, slings his saddlebags over his shoulder, and goes out into the street. The cabmen rush up to offer him their services — he makes a sign with his head that he does not want them. They understand his sign as affirmative, and one cab stops in front of him. Bay Ganyo grows angry, stares, and makes irritated gestures. The policeman notices this and orders the cabs to withdraw. Bay Ganyo thinks to himself whom he could ask to find out where Jireček, our historian, lives. Jireček has lived in Bulgaria, he likes Bulgarians, Bay Ganyo will go to him: “Good day” — “God give you good” — and he may invite him into his house; why should he spend his money on hotels? — While he is thinking thus, a porter with a red cap stops in front of him and offers to carry his saddlebags. Bay Ganyo asks him whether he knows where Jireček lives; the porter answers in the negative, but gives hope that it can be found, and again stretches out his hands to take the saddlebags. Bay Ganyo does not give them to him, first because the flasks are inside and he might “make off somewhere,” and second because he sees that he is well dressed, and who knows how much he will fleece him.

— Your Grace, go ahead, I’ll follow you — says Bay Ganyo politely. — Leave the saddlebags; I’ll carry them. Bay Ganyo puts on this politeness with calculation: he will both predispose the porter in his favor and show him that he is not some great and rich man, so that the other one will not think of fleecing him.

They go around asking at the crossroads where Irechek lives; at last someone remembered that the question was about Professor Irechek, told them where to ask, they asked, and they find him. Bay Ganyo says to the porter a “may you live long, thank you” and enters Irechek’s apartment.

— Oh! Good day, Mr. Yirechek, how are you, are you well? — cries Bay Ganyo in the most friendly tone as soon as he enters the master’s office. The latter extends his hand in surprise, invites him to sit down, and is angry with his memory, which does not remind him who this courteous friend is.

— Don’t you recognize me? — reminds Bay Ganyo, mixing “you” in the formal and informal forms. — Weren’t you a minister in Sofia? — Yes. — Well, I’m from there too! — concludes Bay Ganyo triumphantly. — That’s what you call compatriots, heh, heh, heh, isn’t it? Do you remember the article in the newspaper “Slavyanin”?
— Yes, yes, I remember — replies Jireček in a restrained, condescending tone.

— Boy, they really dirtied you up!... But you just enjoy yourself, don’t worry about it at all! How much I’ve praised you!... They go on saying Jireček this, Jireček that. — “Excuse me,” I say, “that’s not so.”

Irechek knows the Bulgarians well and therefore is in no way surprised by this familiarity of Bay Ganyo. The conversation continues for several minutes in this tone, then moves onto more practical ground: Bay Ganyo praises the landlord’s apartment, hints to him quite pointedly that “at last there is room for even one more strange fellow to settle in here,” talks to him about the hospitality of the Bulgarians, and expresses regret that “look, the others are not like us Bulgarians; if a foreigner enters a Bulgarian house, they will feed him, give him drink, and make up a bed for him.”

Irechek tries to make him understand that the apartment is too small for his household. Bay Ganyo pretends not to hear and develops the theme of Bulgarian hospitality. From this theme the conversation turns to Bay Ganyo’s little trade. He informs the host that he has brought rose oil for sale and tells him: “Tomorrow, if you like, take me to all the factories, I agree; you’ll translate for me, since I don’t know the language, right?”

Irechek hastens to reply that he is not acquainted with the manufacturers of essential oils, since his pursuits are of an entirely different kind, and besides, he has no free time; but he will tell him where the Bulgarian students gather, so that among them someone may be able to help him.

— If you like, sanquim — adds Bay Ganyo — I won’t overburden you. I’ll give the lady too (is she here?) one muskal of oil. I know her too, of course (Ireček cannot stop wondering which lady is meant). And if you have relatives or friends here, tell them that I’ve brought oil — there’s nothing shameful in that! I’ll come around you more often, and we’ll talk about Bulgaria. And if you please, I’m willing to stay at your place as well, while I’m in Prague. Eh?
— Excuse me, but...
— I say, so to speak, if you please — explains Bay Ganyo in a tangled way — it’s better for me at the hotel too, but come on, I said, Yirechek — one of our own...
— Thank you for your attention; I would gladly keep you at home, but I do not have any spare rooms. Today, however, you are our guest and will have lunch with us.
— Let’s have lunch, why shouldn’t we have lunch! — agrees Bay Ganyo. — And your honor, it is said, if not from my table, then from a Bulgarian table you have certainly eaten.

Irechek is occupied with some urgent work, which is interrupted by the entrance of Bay Ganyo. The host sits as if on thorns and does not know how, in a delicate manner, to temporarily send off his loquacious guest. He rings the bell, a servant appears, whom he orders to inform the household that a guest from Bulgaria has arrived. After a little while, his mother comes in. Bay Ganyo barely rises from his chair, makes a double motion with his hand toward his forehead, and condescendingly says: “Oh, hello, all well and good, let’s get to it, ha, like that, in the Bulgarian way. How are you still? I’m glad.”
The lady greeted him kindly and, with a whole series of questions, showed a lively interest in the guest’s homeland.
— Well, tell the truth now — asks Bay Ganyo — where is it nicer, in Prague or in Sofia?

The lady is at a loss; she has not been in Sofia, and Uncle Ganyo, at this question, glances at Jireček with a devilish smile, as if he wants to impress upon him his own view of women: “Well, she’s a woman, isn’t she? What is there to talk to her about?…”

— His Grace will dine at home today — Irchek turns to his mother and then, so that he can continue his work, asks her in German to take Bay Ganyo to another room. The lady suggests to Bay Ganyo that they move into the adjoining room. Bay Ganyo looks piercingly at Irchek, then at the saddle-bags with the muskals, and calculates with his eyebrows: “They said something in German, who knows! But I don’t believe it. After all, he has been a minister in our country. Well, ministers aren’t much good either! But I don’t believe that about him.” — and then he rises hesitantly and goes, at the lady’s direction, toward the adjoining room; but when he reaches the door, he turns around and wants to read on the hosts’ faces their intention, and notices several silent signs that the household members actually exchanged at that moment; these signs meant: “Try to keep him occupied for a longer time, because I have very urgent work,” but Bay Ganyo interpreted them differently.
— These things here may be bothering you — he says, indicating the saddlebags with his eyes.
— Oh, not at all. Please, do not worry — replies Jireček.

— But they’ll still be in your way, I know. Wait, let me take them into the other room — and she reaches out to take them, but the family politely resists. — Am I afraid, no, it’s just that, I said...

They pass into the reception room, and the lady closes the door behind her so that the noise in the office cannot be heard. She tries in every way to occupy Bay Ganyo with something interesting: she offers him various albums, shows him pictures, lays before him a whole pile of illustrations, but Bay Ganyo’s mind is quite elsewhere, and to the lady’s courtesies he replies with feigned indifference:

— No, thank you: you look at them. I’ve looked at such pictures and portraits plenty of times! Don’t let my being young fool you!

Bai Ganyo looks impatiently at his huge silver watch and begins a very interesting and timely conversation:

— I am very curious to study Europe. For example, let us say that with us noon comes — they sit down to lunch. With you it is arranged differently. When do you have lunch, for example?
— We usually have lunch at 5 o’clock, but today we can have lunch earlier too. Excuse me, I’ll leave you for just a minute — said the lady, and went out through the other door.

Bay Ganyo sits alone in the salon, stares absentmindedly at the paintings, spits on the carpet from time to time (not because he is hungry, but who knows!), rubs it with his boots, and listens intently at the slightest noise in the study. At one point he hears Irechek get up from his chair, take a few steps, and stop. “But I’m a fool too, why didn’t I bring my saddlebags into this room?” Bay Ganyo sits on pins and needles; at last he can’t hold out, gets up, tiptoes quietly across the carpet to the study door, bends his ear to the keyhole, and listens; he hears only his own frequent breathing and the pounding of blood in his ears. But even here Bay Ganyo does not calm down, he sees nothing through the keyhole, and as he hesitantly presses the door handle, he opens it, mysteriously pokes his head into the study, and sees Irechek crouched near his saddlebags in front of a bookcase.

Bay Ganyo grins at him: — Hee, hee, hee, are you working, are you working? Hee, hee, hee! Wait, I said, let me peek in. Go on with your work, it’s nothing, I’ll close it again. Jireček looks at him in astonishment, without the reason for this peculiar curiosity even crossing his mind.

Lunch is ready. They go into the dining room and sit around the table: Irechek’s parents, his sister, Bay Ganyo, and he. Bay Ganyo, before the lunch begins, starts making the sign of the cross, while smiling, thereby wanting to show the hosts that he is not one of those simple folk and that he does not really believe that much, but still it is not a bad thing at all (we are on good terms with the devil, so what harm is there in burning a little incense to the Lord too — in case of need).

— I am a liberal, from the Liberal Party — he explains, — but every now and then I have a little sign of the cross; it’s not a bad thing, we’re only human... What is this, is it soup? Ah, I like soup. Chorba is a Turkish dish. And now we eat more soup ourselves. Ah, pardon, excuse me, I’ve soiled your bundle... Tsk... tsk... tsk... Tch, damn it!...

Carried away by the desire to recommend himself as a civilized man, Bay Ganyo could not take straight the plate of soup that the hostess handed him, and spilled quite a bit of it onto the table; and before they could stop him, he gathered some of it with the spoon and poured it into his own plate. The hostess did not want to let him eat that soup, but out of delicacy he shielded his plate with his hands and did not want it to be changed for him.

— I have peppers in my saddlebags — announced Bay Ganyo unexpectedly. He was burning with the desire to rub one of the small peppers into the soup, which seemed quite bland for his stomach, but he was reluctant to take out the peppers, lest they think him a boor, so he wanted to sound out the hosts first.
— Yes? Do you have peppers? — Irechek called out.

— How not, I’ve brought peppers with me; you know, “Dear Mother Bulgaria” can’t do without something spicy — says Bay Ganyo ironically, and without waiting any longer, he jumps up from the chair, goes down into the study, drags in his saddlebags, squats over them with his back to the hosts, and brings two peppers to the table.

— Two are enough for the five of us; they’re terribly hot — he says, shaking half a pepper with the seeds into his plate and politely offering the rest to the hosts: — Here, please, rub it on yourselves, heh, heh, heh, the Bulgarian way! No, no, rub it, listen to me and you’ll see what it’s like. Well, you know: beauty cannot be forced. Wait, let me rub mine, so I can show you what’s called soup.

And indeed, Bay Ganyo had seasoned his soup to such a degree that an unaccustomed person would have been poisoned. And he began to slurp; but when a Bulgarian slurps, he is no joke—three hundred dogs could be fighting and still not drown him out. Large drops of sweat clouded his forehead and seemed about to pour into his plate. Bay Ganyo would slurp once from the tip of the spoon, set the spoon down, and stifle the fiery moisture with two or three bites of bread; then he would take up the spoon again, slurp some soup, sniff inward through his nose, and again two or three bites of bread.

— Give me another little piece of bread. You’re eating completely without bread — бай Ганьо wonders. — Give bread to the Bulgarians; we eat a lot of bread; not to boast, but with such a soup, pardon, with such soup I can eat a whole loaf of bread. I’ll bet on it.
They did not keep bass, but even so Bay Ganyo destroyed quite a bit of bread.
“Where do you get this wine from?” inquired Bay Ganyo, not because he was interested in the answer, but just to find an excuse for another glass.
— We’ll buy it — replies the owner, — is it good?

— Ah! Pure stuff! You’re buying it, eh? Hand me the bottle here. My stomach has been set on fire by the pepper like a red-hot iron; if I pour down the whole bottle now, it’ll sizzle inside. Ah, at home our little wine, half a lev an oka, when you shine a little oka of it — there you are!... Ah, I burped, excuse me: that’s a bit crude, but pardon me, it’s human nature, you can’t hold it in!...

The lunch at Irechek’s, thanks to Bay Ganyo, turned out to be quite lively. They were served coffee in the reception room. Bay Ganyo, in gratitude for the tasty, and above all filling, lunch, wants to treat the host to a cigarette of tobacco, and, as fate would have it, his tobacco is in the saddlebags. To tell the truth, the tobacco box was in his pocket, but he had to find an excuse to go and check on the saddlebags; he simply could not leave his little flasks with strangers like that—anything can happen in this world.
Bay Ganyo does not even want to hear the host’s refusal to let him smoke his tobacco: “How so, my dear, can it be at all possible for a Bulgarian tobacco not to be smoked by a person!”

Silenced, Bay Ganyo began to sip his coffee with relish. Now that is what you call sipping!... To be in such a pleasant mood, to spend whole hours with a companion, to be in a room where no one will hear what you are saying, and even if they do hear, they will not understand you — under such favorable conditions, to hold oneself back and not start talking politics is beyond Bay Ganyo’s powers.

He could not restrain himself; he poured out his soul:

— Well now, Bay Irechek, tell me, your grace, are you a Liberal or a Conservative? I rather think you’re a Conservative, as far as I can see. And I, if you ask me, can’t make heads or tails of either of them, but come on, let’s not offend them... You know, it’s business, trade, that’s what it is, no joke... And should I tell you the plain truth... (Might there not be someone listening to us here?) Should I tell you the plain truth? — Both the one and the other are scoundrels!... Listen to me, and don’t be afraid! They’re all scoundrels, every last one of them!... But what can you do? You can’t kick against the pricks!... I’ve got little businesses, little enterprises, lawsuits in the courts — what can you do? If you’re not with them, you’re done for! And besides, don’t I want it myself — to be elected deputy, or mayor. There’s profit in those things. People have piled up money, do you know that? Fine, but if you don’t tip your hat to them — the devil himself couldn’t get you elected! That’s how it is! I’ve been through and through these things, so I understand them...

Irechek could hardly have doubted that his guest understood “these things.”
